text.p: Tenet Healthcare Corp. said Wednesday it reached an agreement to settle 700 lawsuits brought by former patients who claimed they were admitted to Tenet psychiatric hospitals without cause or were held against their will.
The company did not disclose how much it paid to settle the lawsuits but said it was not significant in terms of its total cash flow.

The New York Times on Wednesday reported Tenet paid about $100 million to settle the lawsuits. Lance Ignon, a Tenet spokesman, would not confirm or deny the amount but he said the financial effect of the settlements on the $9 billion company had been previously disclosed and expected.
Tenet on Thursday is slated to report fourth-quarter earnings, which will include more details on the reserves taken to cover the lawsuits, Ignon said.

The settlements resolve the majority of lawsuits brought against Santa Monica, Calif.-based Tenet by psychiatric patients, whose complaints mainly date back to the early or mid-1980s. Tenet at that time was known as National Medical Enterprises and was under different management.
Ignon said the decision to settle the 700 lawsuits was not an admission of guilt in all cases and said the company had successfully defended itself in an unspecified number of other lawsuits.

With 700 lawsuits settled, there are about 300 still pending by psychiatric patients, some of whom claim they were sent to psychiatric hospitals without ever seeing a doctor and that the company kept them there after they should have been discharged, in order to continue receiving insurance payments.

Also on Wednesday, Dallas-based Timberlawn Psychiatric Hospital announced it was suing Tenet, charging it essentially stole potential psychiatric patients through an aggressive scheme of bribes and kickbacks to psychiatrists and psychologists who referred patients to Tenet-run hospitals rather than facilities run by competitors.

Timberlawn says Tenet's alleged practices helped drive Timberlawn into bankruptcy. The company reorganized in 1994 and was acquired by Universal Health Services. Timberlawn is suing for at least $50 million in damages and seeking to have that amount tripled under federal racketeering laws.
Tenet's Ignon said the Timberlawn lawsuit was unrelated to others filed by patients, and represented "a financially troubled company looking for an excuse for its problems."

The settlements were negotiated as Tenet entered talks to buy Columbia/HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the nation. But those talks were put on hold as Columbia became the target of a sweeping criminal investigation. The government announced Wednesday that three Columbia executives have been indicted on fraud charges.
Tenet stock was unchanged Wednesday at $31 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
